tldr: Three papers in six days audit the measurements behind agent and model evaluation rather than the models. First came trace-derived labels, then a headline memory gain in XLand-MiniGrid.
whats_new: A new paper tests model self-confidence and LLM-as-a-judge as cheaper ways to audit human-in-the-loop evaluation, aiming for statistically sound accuracy estimates.
why_it_matters: Agent eval scores are only as good as the labels and noise floors behind them; if parsers, detectors, seeds or judges are unreliable, regressions and gains in your CI evals can be artifacts.
take_for_builders: Audit your own eval harness: spot-check detector labels against raw traces, rerun headline gains across seeds and maps, and calibrate any LLM judge against a human-labeled sample before trusting it.

beats.headline: Trace-derived labels are measurements, not ground truth
beats.summary: Behavioral detectors and parsers that turn agent traces into labels need their own audit.

beats.headline: A 25-point memory gain gets audited against seeds, maps and noise
Self-confidence and LLM judges proposed to scale human-in-the-loop audits

open_questions: Do agent benchmarks begin publishing detector and label audits alongside scores?
Does LLM-assisted auditing hold its accuracy estimates on agentic traces, not just single-turn outputs?
